groups.title: Cross-Origin Communication
groups.question: Your React app on localhost:5173 calls your Django API on localhost:8000, and POST requests fail with CORS and CSRF errors. Explain what is happening and how you would fix it.

followUps.CORS Configuration in Django: Why does the browser block the React app's request, and how does django-cors-headers fix it?
followUps.CSRF Tokens and API Safety: When does Django require a CSRF token, and when can an API skip it?

evidence.text: Different ports are different origins, so the browser blocks reading the response by default.
django-cors-headers adds CORS headers that allow chosen origins.
Its middleware must be added and the React origin listed explicitly.
With session or cookie authentication, unsafe requests like POST need a CSRF token.
The token proves the request came from your own site and not a forged one.
APIs that use tokens in headers instead of cookies are not exposed the same way.

notEnough: Only saying CSRF tokens are required.

groups.title: Handling Async State in React
groups.question: Your React recipe pages need to show loading and errors, create and edit recipes, and page through hundreds of results from DRF. Explain how you would handle each.

followUps.Loading and Error State Patterns: How would you model the states of a request in the UI?
followUps.Posting and Updating Data to APIs: After creating a recipe, how do you update the list?
followUps.Client-Side Pagination with APIs: How would the frontend use DRF's pagination data?

evidence.text: A request is loading, successful or failed.
A single status value drives what is rendered.
Each state has its own UI, such as a spinner or an error message.

notEnough: Only saying you show a spinner.

evidence.text: Send the data as JSON with the right content type.
Use POST to create and PUT or PATCH to update.
On success, refetch the list or add the returned item to state.

notEnough: Only saying you post the data.

evidence.text: DRF returns the count and next and previous URLs with each page.
The current page is kept in state.
The frontend fetches the next or previous URL and shows page controls.

groups.title: Axios HTTP Client
groups.question: Fetch calls with full URLs and headers are copied across your React app, and every component handles 401 errors differently. Explain how an Axios setup fixes this.

followUps.Creating an Axios Instance with Base URL: Why create one Axios instance for the app?
followUps.Axios Interceptors for Error Handling: What can request and response interceptors do?

evidence.text: An instance sets the base URL and default headers once.
It is exported from one file and used everywhere.
Changing the API URL or headers then happens in one place.
A request interceptor can attach the auth header to every request.
A response interceptor can handle errors like 401 in one place.
It can also refresh tokens before the error reaches components.

groups.title: Environment Configuration
groups.question: Your API URL is hard-coded to localhost and a developer committed the Django secret key. Explain how you would configure both apps and avoid CORS in development.

followUps.Environment Variables in Vite and Django: How do Vite and Django read environment variables?
followUps.Proxy Configuration for Local Developmen: How does a Vite proxy remove CORS problems in development?

evidence.text: Vite exposes only variables prefixed with VITE_ to the browser code.
Django reads variables from the environment or a .env file through a helper library.
.env files with secrets are never committed.

misconceptions.text: Says secrets in VITE_ variables are hidden from users.

evidence.text: The Vite dev server forwards /api requests to Django.
The browser sees only one origin, so no CORS rules apply.
It is only for local development.

notEnough: Only saying you configure a proxy.
